opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and it gets at something I've been thinking about for most of my career.

If you look at how we've built computers for the last seventy-plus years, the whole paradigm rests on control. We take physical systems, transistors and electrons that are inherently noisy and stochastic, and we spend an enormous amount of energy suppressing that noise. We force them into clean, deterministic zeros and ones. Then, on top of that perfectly controlled substrate, we write software that tries to simulate randomness again: sampling, Monte Carlo methods, diffusion models, Bayesian inference. We pay twice. We pay energy to kill the noise, and then we pay compute to fake it back.

That made sense when computation meant arithmetic, spreadsheets, ballistics tables. But the workloads that matter now, especially in AI, are fundamentally probabilistic. Generative models are learning and sampling from distributions. Nature already does that natively. A physical system in contact with a heat bath explores its state space and relaxes toward equilibrium distributions for free, as a consequence of thermodynamics.

So when I say we should loosen our grip, I mean we should stop fighting physics and start using it. Instead of programming every step, you shape the energy landscape of a physical system, by setting its couplings and parameters, and let the dynamics do the computation. You give up micromanaging each bit, and you gain orders of magnitude in efficiency, because the computation emerges from the physics rather than being imposed against it.

I think there's a broader philosophical point too. Software has gone through the same transition. We moved from hand-written rules, expert systems where a human specified everything, to learned systems where we specify an objective and let optimization find the solution. That was a loss of control in a sense: we don't fully understand every weight in a neural network. But it unlocked capabilities we could never have hand-engineered. Hardware is the next layer of that stack. If you let the substrate itself be adaptive, stochastic, and self-organizing, you open a much larger design space.

And frankly, I'd extend that to how we think about technological progress and civilization more broadly. Complex adaptive systems tend to outperform top-down, centrally planned ones because they can explore and adapt in ways a planner can't anticipate. There's a tension there, obviously, and people worry about losing control. But I think the right move is to design good constraints and incentives, a good energy landscape if you like, rather than trying to dictate every outcome. That's how nature produced everything interesting we see around us, including us.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the way we've built computing historically has been about imposing our will on physics. We take a system that's inherently noisy, inherently stochastic, and we spend enormous amounts of energy forcing it into a deterministic box. Error correction, clock synchronization, keeping transistors in clean binary states. All of that costs you. It costs you energy, it costs you time, and increasingly it's hitting fundamental limits.

And it's kind of funny if you step back, because the physics itself doesn't want to be deterministic. Nature is doing computation all the time, at the atomic scale, at the thermal scale, and it does it with noise as a resource rather than as an enemy. Biological systems run on fluctuations. Your brain is a wet, noisy, thermally messy thing, and it does intelligence at something like twenty watts.

So my view is that the next phase of computing is about relaxing. Instead of fighting the noise, you design hardware where the natural dynamics of the physical system are the computation. You let thermodynamics do the sampling for you. A lot of modern machine learning is essentially probabilistic inference, sampling from distributions, and we're currently simulating that randomness on deterministic chips, which is backwards. You're paying to generate entropy that the universe would give you for free.

And the same philosophy scales up to software and to how we think about intelligence more broadly. Rigidly controlled systems are brittle. The systems that adapt, that search, that explore the space of possibilities, are the ones that survive and grow. So loosening control isn't about being reckless, it's about aligning with how the universe already computes. You get more capability per joule, and I'd argue you get something closer to how intelligence actually works.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve built computing around the idea that we should specify exactly what happens at every step. That’s extraordinarily useful for making reliable machines, but it also constrains the kinds of processes we can exploit. We ask the physics to behave like a clean, deterministic abstraction, and then spend energy suppressing everything that doesn’t fit that abstraction.

With machine learning, we’ve already loosened that grip at the software level. We don’t write down every rule for recognising an image; we set up a learning process and let it discover a solution. We still choose the objective and the constraints, but we give up prescribing the implementation in detail.

You can imagine extending that attitude down into the hardware. Instead of treating fluctuations, noise, and collective behaviour solely as things to eliminate, could we build systems in which those dynamics do useful computational work? Let the physical system explore possibilities, and engineer how we steer it and read out the result.

The challenge is knowing where to relinquish control. You still need interfaces you can trust and ways to check whether the system is doing what you want. But demanding control over every microscopic step may prevent you from discovering a much more efficient way to compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we tend to equate control with understanding. In software, we want every operation to be specified, every state transition to be predictable. And in hardware, we put a tremendous amount of effort into making physical devices behave like these ideal, deterministic switches. That abstraction is incredibly useful, but maintaining it has a cost.

The physical world has fluctuations, noise, and all these interacting degrees of freedom. You can spend energy suppressing them, or you can ask whether some of that dynamics can actually do useful computation. Then your job becomes less about prescribing every microscopic step and more about shaping the conditions so that useful behavior emerges.

Machine learning already asks us to make a version of that trade. We specify an architecture, an objective, and a learning process, but we don't write down the algorithm the trained system ultimately implements. We give up some direct control to access a much larger space of possible solutions.

So I wouldn't say abandon control. I'd say put control at the right level. Constrain what matters, measure whether the system does what you need, and allow flexibility underneath. Otherwise, we risk spending most of our resources forcing the substrate to obey our preferred model of computation, rather than discovering what it can do.
